title: Ordering food
goal: Order, pay, and make small talk in a restaurant, and master the suffix *-аар / -ээр*, which means "with," "by way of," and "in (a language)."
bekal: order food and drinks, and ask what's in a dish
use the suffix *-аар* for tools, manner, routes, and languages
decline, ask for more, and ask for the bill politely

dialogs.title: Яриа — Рестораны цэсэнд

notes: ⚠️ **The suffix -аар / -ээр / -оор / -өөр does four jobs at once:** tool (*махаар*, with meat), manner (*бичгээр*, in writing), route (*замаар*, along the road), and language (*монголоор*, in Mongolian). They all answer the question "by what?", so think of it as one suffix with one flexible meaning.

**Монголоор ярих = to speak in Mongolian.** ⚠️ Notice that the suffix goes on *монгол*, not on *хэл*. Saying *монгол хэлээр* is also correct but sounds more formal; in conversation people say *монголоор*, *англиар*, *оросоор*, *индонезоор*.
**Өгнө үү literally means "will you give?" and works exactly like "please."** *Ус өгнө үү* = water, please. It's the most polite way to ask and can be paired with any verb.

**The suffix -аарай / -ээрэй is a polite, warm command**, used for suggestions and wishes: *нэмээрэй* (please add), *сайхан хооллоорой* (enjoy your meal), *сайн яваарай* (have a safe trip). It sounds like a friendly "won't you?" or "okay?" at the end of an English sentence: it softens without changing the content.

**Тооцоо = bill, check.** *Тооцоог авъя* or *тооцоо хийе* is how you ask for the bill. ⚠️ In Mongolia, tipping isn't yet a general custom except in expensive restaurants in Ulaanbaatar; if the service was good, rounding up is more than enough.

grammars.title: The suffix -аар: with, by way of, in
body: Four forms follow vowel harmony, chosen exactly as for the other suffixes you already know.
after: **The four most common uses, with examples you can use right away:**

⚠️ *Автобус**аар** явна* (go by bus): notice that Mongolian says "go **by** bus," much as English does. The verb *явах* handles every means of transport: *машинаар*, *онгоцоор* (by plane), *галт тэргээр* (by train), *явганаар* (on foot).

grammars.title: Asking politely: three levels
body: Mongolian has three ways to ask, and the difference is like the difference between "take it," "please take it," and "could you please take it" in English.

after: ⚠️ **Битгий is the only way to say "don't" in Mongolian, and it goes IN FRONT of the verb**: the only thing besides the object allowed to stand before the verb. *Битгий хоцроорой* = don't be late, okay?

The *-аарай* form is the most useful to learn first, because it's never out of place: polite enough for strangers, warm enough for friends. **If you memorize only one command form from this unit, make it this one.**

blocks.text: ⚠️ Notice the pattern for meats: **animal with -ын/-ийн + мах**. *Хонь* (sheep) → *хонины мах*; *үхэр* (cow) → *үхрийн мах*; *тахиа* (chicken) → *тахианы мах*. Literally "the sheep's meat." Once you know the animal, you know the meat, unlike English, which uses completely different words (*sheep* and *mutton*).

blocks.title: ⚠️ If you don't eat pork or are looking for halal food
items: *Гахайн мах* (ga-KHAIN makh) = pork. The sentence to memorize: ***Би гахайн мах иддэггүй.*** — I don't eat pork.

Traditional Mongolian cooking is almost entirely **mutton and beef**; pork is far rarer than in China or Korea, so the risk is small. What to watch out for is Korean- and Chinese-style cooking in the city.
Ulaanbaatar has a Kazakh Muslim community and several halal restaurants, especially around *Баянгол* and in the Kazakh region of *Баян-Өлгий* province.
*Би мах иддэггүй.* — I don't eat meat. ⚠️ Be ready to explain; vegetarianism is still very unusual in Mongolia, and the questions will be sincere, not judgmental.

blocks.text: Notice that **Mongolian has no phrase said before eating** by the eater, like Japanese *itadakimasu*. *Сайхан хооллоорой* is said **to** the person about to eat, by the waiter or host, like "Enjoy your meal." If you're the one eating, just reply *баярлалаа*.

⚠️ Notice the suffixes **-тай** (having) and **-гүй** (lacking) that form most of these adjectives: *амт* (taste) → *амттай* (tasty) and *амтгүй* (tasteless). This pattern is very productive, and you can use it to make new adjectives yourself: *мөнгөтэй* (having money, rich), *мөнгөгүй* (penniless), *цагтай* (having time), *цаггүй* (having no time).

One note on flavor that often surprises visitors: **Mongolian cooking uses almost no chili, garlic, or spices at all.** The seasoning is salt, and sometimes onion. It isn't a shortcoming but a choice: in a climate where vegetables barely grow for eight months a year, the flavor comes from the meat itself. If you like it hot, bring your own hot sauce; that's what many foreigners living there do.
